nameStory: The American crow gets its name from its distinctive harsh "caw-caw" call that sounds like the word "crow." The word "crow" comes from Old English "crawe," which was meant to imitate the bird's voice. They're called "American" to distinguish them from their Old World cousins like the carrion crow and hooded crow of Europe and Asia.
description: The American crow is a large, intelligent black bird that's one of the most familiar sights across New England. These sturdy birds are about the size of a small chicken, with glossy all-black feathers that shimmer with blue and purple when the light hits them just right. They're highly adaptable and equally at home in wild forests, suburban neighborhoods, and busy city parks. Their sharp intelligence and bold personality make them one of nature's most successful survivors.

idTips.label: All-black plumage
idTips.description: Completely black from head to toe with a subtle rainbow sheen - hold your hand up next to them and notice how their feathers catch purple, blue, and green highlights in sunlight

idTips.label: Distinctive call
idTips.description: Classic harsh "caw-caw-caw" that carries far - sounds rough and grating, like someone clearing their throat loudly

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Robust bird about 17-21 inches long with a thick, sturdy body that looks substantial when perched - bigger than a robin, smaller than a goose

idTips.label: Straight, thick bill
idTips.description: Heavy black beak that's straight and pointed, not curved like a hawk's - looks like a sturdy tool built for versatile eating

idTips.label: Confident behavior
idTips.description: Walks boldly on the ground with a strutting gait, often in groups, showing little fear of humans - watch them hop and walk with obvious intelligence in their movements

habitat: American crows thrive everywhere from deep wilderness forests to downtown city streets across New England. You'll spot them in open woodlands, agricultural fields, suburban lawns, parking lots, beaches, and park spaces. They're particularly drawn to areas where forests meet open spaces, and anywhere humans provide easy food sources like garbage, bird feeders, or outdoor dining areas.

seasonality.spring: Crows become more vocal and active as they build stick nests high in trees and defend territories. Listen for increased calling and watch for pairs gathering nesting materials like twigs and string.
seasonality.summer: Family groups become obvious as parents lead their slightly smaller, begging young around in search of food. The young have a distinctive raspy begging call that's different from adult caws.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks begin forming as families join together for winter, creating impressive gatherings of dozens or hundreds of birds. Their calls become a constant background chorus in many areas.
seasonality.winter: Massive communal roosts form where thousands of crows gather to sleep together, creating spectacular dawn and dusk flights. They're often the most visible large bird in snowy landscapes.

funFact: American crows can learn to mimic human speech even better than some parrots, and wild crows have been observed crafting tools from twigs to fish insects out of tree bark - making them one of the few animals that both use and manufacture tools in the wild.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with ravens, but ravens are much larger with shaggier throat feathers and a deeper, croaking call that sounds like "kronk-kronk." Remember: if you're not sure if it's a crow or raven, it's probably a crow - ravens are less common and much more impressive in size. Fish crows look nearly identical but have a more nasal "uh-uh" call instead of the classic caw.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their association with bad omens in European folklore, many Native American cultures consider crows symbols of intelligence and good fortune. These birds have thrived alongside human development and are actually more common now than they were 100 years ago, making them a rare wildlife success story in our increasingly developed landscape.
compareHints: American crows are smaller and more slender than Common ravens, which have wedge-shaped tails and shaggier throat feathers. They're nearly identical to Fish crows but have that classic harsh caw instead of the Fish crow's more nasal call. Unlike ravens that soar like hawks, crows typically fly with steady wingbeats and rarely soar except in strong winds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to American Crows, Ravens are significantly larger with wedge-shaped tails, deeper voices, and preference for wild areas over suburbs.
Fish Crows are smaller and more coastal than American Crows, with that distinctive nasal call being the most reliable difference.
